newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK's Patten defends deportation of children.
newsitem.headline: HK's Patten defends deportation of children.

text.p: Hong Kong Governor Chris Patten on Thursday defended a decision to seize an eight-year-old girl and her mother from their family home and deport them, saying immigration rules must be followed.
In an unusual display of force, Hong Kong immigration officers plucked Chung Yeuk-lam and her mother, both illegal immigrants, from their home on Tuesday morning and drove them to the Chinese border.
The move has sparked a big debate in Hong Kong over the backlog of tens of thousands of mainland children waiting to join their immigrant parents in Hong Kong.
The debate spilled into the territory's Legislature on Thursday when legislators asked Patten why the government had to be so tough with mainland children.

"Because the moment that we back off, the moment that we are not prepared to see a policy through is the moment when the snakeheads...are able to increase the credibility across the border that there may be some change in policy," Patten told the legislature.
Hundreds of Hong Kong parents pay smugglers, or snakeheads, to spirit China-born children into the British colony.

Yeuk-lam and her China-born mother snuck into Hong Kong when the girl was three months old. She was deported once before but her father brought her back and she had spent most of her life in Hong Kong.
Hong Kong runs a quota system agreed with China, letting 150 mainland-born children in each day to join their families.
Hong Kong's future leader Tung Chee-hwa vowed on Monday that the rules would not be eased after the handover of Hong Kong to China on July 1 and that smuggled children would be deported.
He plans to visit the south China city of Guangzhou on Sunday to discuss the problem with officials there.
Social workers estimate anywhere from 30,000 to 130,000 children living in China might be eligible to be reunited with families in Hong Kong.

Most of them have Hong Kong fathers and mainland mothers. Both the mothers and the children have to apply through Chinese authorities for the right to leave and go to Hong Kong -- a process which can take many years.
